messages.subject: Fluctuating asymmetry with individual covariates
parts:
Dear geomorph list:


I am assessing shape variation in damselflies wings that live in oligotrophic and eutrophic lakes and one of my goals is to evaluate fluctuating asymmetry as a proxy of the individuals' condition and environmental stress they suffer.


Using bilat.symmetry function separately for the two populations, I have found that individuals of both lakes possess directional and fluctuating asymmetry in the anterior wings but the posterior wings are asymmetric only in the eutrophic lake. I would like to include the levels of ectoparasitism (number aquatic mites each individual carry) to see if it is related with the degree of asymmetry damselflies show. Since bilat.symmetry function does not have an argument to include continuous variables I was wondering how to proceed.


I have read in the great geomorph manual that you can extract the asymmetric components of shape and that they can be used in subsequent analyses, but I would be very grateful if someone could advise me how to do it.


a) Can I perform a MANCOVA in R using the asymmetric components of shape of both populations as a response variable having as predictors: a categorical (population origin) and a continuous variable (number of parasites)?


b) If that is the case, should I pool the individuals of both populations before the bilat.symmetry analysis or I would merge the asymmetric components of shape that are the result of two separate analyses for each population?


b) Do I have to correct the degrees of freedom for these analyses?


Thanks for your help,


Roberto Munguía-Steyer

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Fluctuating asymmetry with individual covariates
parts:
Roberto,

 

It is best to pool the samples prior to the bilat.asymmetry analysis, as this function also performs the Procrustes superimposition, which should be done on all specimens simultaneously.

 

Once that is completed you can output the asymmetric shape components for further analysis; say, comparing the degree of asymmetry in different levels of ectoparasitism, etc.

 

As for df and MANCOVA, if the above analysis is performed using procD.lm, this is a permutation-based MANCOVA, so that is much less of an issue. For parametric assessment of significance, df matter a great deal, but that is not what is implemented in geomorph.

 

Dean

parts:
Hi Dean, thanks for your kind reply.

Checking the structure of the model, I see that I can extract the
asymmetric component of shape but also just the FA asymmetry:

anteriores_sim <- bilat.symmetry(land, ind = ind, side = side,
replicate=replicate, object.sym = FALSE, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 1000, data
= anteriores_gdf)

# Directional and FA asymmetry
anteriores_sim$asymm.shape

# Just FA asymmetry
fa_sim <- anteriores_sim$FA.component

Is it okay then just to import other predictors such as parasitism and
then use procD.lm function to assess if individuals with more parasites
are more prone to show fluctuating asymmetry?

#parasite data base
bd <- read.table("ha.csv", sep=",", header=T)
parasites <- bd$ectopar

m1 <- procD.lm(fa_sim ~parasites)
summary(m1)

and the last question, if I am testing FA both in shape and size, is
there a way to extract from the model the fluctuating asymmetry values
for the centroid size analysis?


Roberto

Roberto,

Yes, one may import other predictors for a subsequent anova-type analysis. This makes perfect sense to do if one wishes to investigate whether levels of shape asymmetry differ across groups.

As for size, at present the function does not output the size components.
